pages.title: Design current, Ib
pages.for: The current the circuit carries in normal service (slides p.11). The device and the cable are chosen from it, and every check after them starts from that choice.
pages.rule:
Single-phase: Ib = P ÷ (U × eff × pf)
Three-phase: Ib = P ÷ (√3 × UL × eff × pf)

P is the output in watts. U is the voltage at the board when you are given one; otherwise 230 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase (slides p.12, 13, 18).
A heater like the slides' 20 kW one is worked with both as 1 (p.16); a motor's come from its nameplate or the maker's data (p.14).
In delta, each winding carries the line current ÷ √3.

traps.text: Sizing on the output alone: 28.87 A where the load draws 41.48 A.
230 V or 400 V by habit when the board's voltage is given.
Diversity treated as a rule: it is guidance, from the On-Site Guide.

pages.where: your slides p.10 to 19; the formula sheet, step 1; the flowchart, step 1; diversity in the On-Site Guide, Appendix A (slides p.10).

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: Design current, [[Ib]], is "the magnitude of the current to be carried by a circuit in normal service" (your slides p.11). The device and the cable are chosen from it, and every check after them starts from that choice.
pages.alt: YOUR SLIDES P.22 Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz The design current, no more than the device's rating, no more than what the cable can carry. If it is skipped or wrong: every later step starts from the wrong current.
pages.html:
Your slides p.22

Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz

The design current, no more than the device's rating, no more than what the cable can carry.

If it is skipped or wrong: every later step starts from the wrong current.

pages.name: The why
pages.text: The cable carries what the load [[draws from the supply]], not what it gives out. Your slides take P as the load's output and put the [[efficiency]] in the rule (p.12, 13), so the losses add to the draw; reactance, behind the [[power factor]], adds to it too (p.15).
pages.alt: The same 20 kW output at 400 V. Drag either one. Output 20.00 kW Input = output ÷ efficiency 22.99 kW Apparent = input ÷ power factor 28.74 kVA Ib, from the apparent power 41.48 A 28.74 kVA × 1000 ÷ (√3 × 400) Losses stretch the input past the output, and reactance stretches the apparent power past the input. The line current follows the apparent power: 12.61 A more than the output alone needs. If it's skipped: the cable is sized on 28.87 A when the load draws 41.48 A, which your slides say "would cause big implications for the operation and safety of the circuit" (p.17). Real, apparent and reactive power are the AC circuits course's lesson 8; here they only show where the extra current comes from.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: A 7.5 kW three-phase motor on a 400 V supply, power factor 0.85, efficiency 90%. What is Ib?
pages.why: Ib = P ÷ (√3 × UL × eff × pf) (your slides p.13): 7 500 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.9 × 0.85) = 14.15 A. Leave out the efficiency and you get 12.74 A; leave out the power factor and you get 12.03 A.
pages.html:
That's it.

7 500 ÷ (√3 × 400 × 0.9 × 0.85) = 14.15 A

pages.name: The voltage at the board
pages.text: If you are given a voltage for the board, that voltage must be used (your slides p.18). At a sub-board it is lower than 400 V, because the submain drops some on the way, so the same power works out at more current. Your slides work it as if the load still takes its full power: near enough for a motor driving its load, and for a plain heater, which really draws a little less at a lower voltage, the figure errs on the safe side.
pages.alt: MDB 400 V submain voltage drop Sub-board 393 V final circuit 20 kW load Worked at 400 V (p.16) 20 000 ÷ (√3 × 400) = 28.87 A Worked at the board's 393 V (p.19) 20 000 ÷ (√3 × 393) = 29.38 A Diversity, in two lines: the On-Site Guide's percentages are guidance and need not be applied (your slides p.10). On a domestic lighting circuit its Appendix A allows 66%, so ten 100 W lamps may be designed at 10 × 100 × 0.66 = 660 W rather than 1000 W. Lesson 2 does more.

pages.name: Section A (b)
pages.task: The same motor, its line current 23.08 A from part (a). (b) Determine the current in each winding when the motor runs in delta.
pages.why: 23.08 ÷ √3 = 13.33 A. In a balanced delta the line current is the winding current × √3 (Lessons in Electric Circuits, AC chapter 10), so each winding carries the line current ÷ √3. Your showroom's motor has a star-delta starter (pack p.4), which runs six wires to the motor, one to each end of each winding (an answer on the PLCtalk forum), so in delta each of those cables carries one winding's current. Lesson 3 sizes them, as question 4b asks.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain why Ib for a final circuit fed from a sub-board is worked at the voltage at that board, not at 400 V.
pages.why: A model answer: The submain between the main board and the sub-board drops some voltage, so the sub-board sits below 400 V (your slides p.18). Your slides work the load at the same power, so a lower voltage gives a larger current, since Ib = P ÷ (√3 × U): their 20 kW load is 28.87 A at 400 V but 29.38 A at 393 V (p.16, 19). That is near enough for a motor and errs on the safe side for a plain heater, which really draws a little less. The device and the cable are chosen from Ib (Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, p.22), so working at 400 V would pick both on too small a current.
